title: Assessment: How Do You Know a Reaction Happened?
description: Checkpoint assessment on identifying indicators of chemical reactions and distinguishing chemical changes from physical changes.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a chemical reaction?
options: A substance changes size but keeps the same properties.
A substance changes state from solid to liquid.
Atoms are rearranged to form one or more new substances.
A material is moved from one container to another.
questions.explanation: In a chemical reaction, atoms are rearranged and new substances with new properties are formed.

questions.question: Two clear liquids are mixed. The mixture becomes cloudy and a white solid settles at the bottom. What indicator is shown?
questions.explanation: A solid forming from mixed solutions is a precipitate, which is a common indicator of a chemical reaction.

questions.question: True or False: A physical change can change the appearance of a material without forming a new substance.
questions.explanation: Physical changes can alter size, shape, or state, but the material's identity stays the same.

questions.question: Which example is most likely a physical change?
questions.explanation: Broken glass is still glass. Its shape changed, but no new substance necessarily formed.

questions.question: A sealed cold pack becomes colder after it is squeezed. Which indicator is being observed?
questions.explanation: A temperature change that happens on its own after materials mix can indicate that a chemical process is absorbing or releasing energy.

questions.question: The starting substances in a chemical reaction are called ________.
questions.explanation: Reactants are the substances present before the reaction. They change into products.

questions.question: The new substances formed in a chemical reaction are called ________.
questions.explanation: Products are the substances formed by a chemical reaction.

questions.question: True or False: A color change is always proof that a chemical reaction happened.
questions.explanation: A color change can be a clue, but it is not always proof. Mixing colored dyes can change color without making a new substance.

questions.question: Which situation shows gas release as evidence of a chemical reaction rather than boiling?
options: Water bubbles after being heated to its boiling point.
Vinegar and baking soda fizz at room temperature.
Water vapor appears on a bathroom mirror.
questions.explanation: Vinegar and baking soda produce carbon dioxide gas at room temperature. This gas is a new product of a chemical reaction.

questions.question: Name three common indicators of a chemical reaction.
questions.correctAnswer: Examples include color change, formation of a precipitate, release of gas, production of odor, and temperature change.
questions.explanation: Any three of the five lesson indicators are acceptable: color change, precipitate formation, gas release, odor production, or temperature change.

questions.question: A banana peel turns dark over time. Explain why this may be evidence of a chemical change.
questions.correctAnswer: The darkening is a color change caused by reactions with substances in the banana peel and oxygen in the air, forming new substances.
questions.explanation: The important idea is that the color change is connected to new substances forming, not just a change in shape or state.

questions.question: Why should you ask whether a new substance formed before deciding that a change is chemical?
questions.correctAnswer: Many physical changes also look noticeable, such as melting, boiling, cutting, or dissolving. A chemical change requires formation of a new substance with new properties.
questions.explanation: Indicators are clues, but the strongest test is whether reactants became products with new properties.
